content.text: As problems grow larger and more complex, single-computer sequential processing becomes impractical — either because it takes too long, or because the problem is too large to fit in one computer's memory. This topic covers three computational models and how to compare their efficiency: sequential computing, parallel computing, and distributed computing.

content.definition: A computational model in which operations are performed in order one at a time. A sequential solution takes as long as the sum of all of its steps.

content.text: Sequential computing is the simplest model — one operation happens, finishes, then the next begins. No operations overlap. The total time is simply the sum of every step's time. This is how most programs you have written in Unit 3 work: statement by statement, in order.

content.code:
-- Sequential computing time calculation:
-- Task A takes 10 seconds
-- Task B takes 20 seconds
-- Task C takes 15 seconds
-- Run one at a time in order:

Total sequential time = 10 + 20 + 15 = 45 seconds

-- A sequential solution takes as long as the SUM of all its steps

content.definition: A computational model where the program is broken into multiple smaller sequential computing operations, some of which are performed simultaneously. A parallel computing solution takes as long as its sequential tasks plus the longest of its parallel tasks.

content.text: Parallel computing breaks a program into parts and runs some of those parts simultaneously on multiple processors or cores. The key insight is that only INDEPENDENT tasks can run in parallel — tasks that depend on the result of another task must still wait. This means every parallel solution still has a sequential portion.

content.term: How to calculate the time for a parallel computing solution
content.definition:
Time = sequential tasks + longest parallel task.
Example: if sequential tasks take 5 seconds and parallel tasks take 3, 4, and 6 seconds simultaneously, total time = 5 + 6 = 11 seconds.

content.code:
-- Parallel computing time calculation:
-- Sequential setup: 5 seconds (MUST run first)
-- Parallel task A: 10 seconds  ┐
-- Parallel task B: 25 seconds  ├── run simultaneously
-- Parallel task C: 15 seconds  ┘
-- Sequential cleanup: 3 seconds (MUST run after parallel tasks)

-- Parallel time = sequential tasks + LONGEST parallel task
-- Total = (5 + 3) + 25
-- Total = 8 + 25 = 33 seconds

-- Compare to sequential:
-- Sequential total = 5 + 10 + 25 + 15 + 3 = 58 seconds
-- Parallel saves: 58 - 33 = 25 seconds

content.label: Exam Tip
content.text: Parallel time = sequential portion + LONGEST parallel task. The other parallel tasks finish before the longest one — they do not add to the total time. ONLY the longest parallel task determines the parallel portion's contribution to total time.

content.definition:
Speedup = sequential time / parallel time.
Example: if a task takes 20 seconds sequentially but 5 seconds in parallel, the speedup is 20 / 5 = 4. This means the parallel solution is 4 times faster.

content.text: Speedup measures how much faster the parallel solution is compared to the sequential one. A speedup of 2 means the parallel solution is twice as fast. A speedup of 10 means ten times as fast. The speedup is calculated by dividing the sequential time by the parallel time.

content.code:
-- Speedup calculation examples:

-- Example 1:
-- Sequential time: 60 seconds
-- Parallel time: 20 seconds
-- Speedup = 60 / 20 = 3
-- The parallel solution is 3 times faster

-- Example 2:
-- Sequential time: 100 seconds
-- Parallel time: 25 seconds
-- Speedup = 100 / 25 = 4
-- The parallel solution is 4 times faster

-- Example 3 (from time calculation above):
-- Sequential time: 58 seconds
-- Parallel time: 33 seconds
-- Speedup = 58 / 33 ≈ 1.76
-- The parallel solution is about 1.76 times faster

content.definition: Every parallel computing solution still has a sequential portion. The efficiency of the overall solution is limited by that sequential portion — at some point, adding more parallel processes will no longer meaningfully increase efficiency.

content.term: When does adding more parallel processes stop helping?
content.definition: When increasing parallel computing in a solution, efficiency is still limited by the sequential portion. At some point, adding more parallel processes will no longer meaningfully increase efficiency because the sequential bottleneck remains constant.

content.text: This is one of the most important and commonly tested concepts in topic 4.3. Every parallel solution has two parts: a parallel portion (which benefits from more processors) and a sequential portion (which cannot be parallelized and must always run serially). No matter how many processors you add, the sequential portion always takes the same amount of time. Eventually, the sequential portion becomes the bottleneck — adding more parallel processors stops making the overall solution meaningfully faster.

content.code:
-- Demonstrating the sequential bottleneck:
-- Sequential portion: 40 seconds (CANNOT be parallelized)
-- Parallel portion: 60 seconds of work

-- With 1 processor (sequential only):
-- Total = 40 + 60 = 100 seconds

-- With 2 processors (parallel work split in half):
-- Total = 40 + 30 = 70 seconds  (speedup: 100/70 ≈ 1.43)

-- With 4 processors:
-- Total = 40 + 15 = 55 seconds  (speedup: 100/55 ≈ 1.82)

-- With 10 processors:
-- Total = 40 + 6 = 46 seconds   (speedup: 100/46 ≈ 2.17)

-- With 100 processors:
-- Total = 40 + 0.6 = 40.6 seconds (speedup: 100/40.6 ≈ 2.46)

-- With INFINITE processors:
-- Total = 40 + 0 = 40 seconds   (speedup: 100/40 = 2.5 MAX)

-- No matter how many processors: speedup CANNOT exceed 100/40 = 2.5
-- The 40-second sequential portion is the permanent bottleneck

content.label: Key Idea
content.text: Parallel computing consists of a parallel portion AND a sequential portion. The sequential portion sets a ceiling on how fast the solution can ever be, regardless of how many processors are added. This is why at some point, adding more parallel processes will no longer meaningfully increase efficiency — the sequential bottleneck dominates.

content.definition: A computational model in which multiple devices are used to run a program. Allows problems to be solved that could not be solved on a single computer because of processing time or storage needs. Allows much larger problems to be solved more quickly.

content.text: Distributed computing goes beyond parallel computing on one machine — it uses multiple separate physical devices (computers) working together on a single problem. This is particularly important for two types of problems: problems that take too long for one computer to solve in a reasonable time, and problems whose data is too large to fit in one computer's storage.

rows: Processing time too long for one computer
Analyzing the entire human genome for disease markers across millions of patients
Would take years on one computer — distributed across thousands completes in days
Storage needs exceed one computer's capacity
Indexing every web page on the Internet (like Google does)
One computer cannot store an index of the entire Web — must be distributed across many machines
Training a large AI model on a massive data set
Data too large for one machine, computation too slow for one processor — needs distributed systems

content.term: Compare: Sequential vs Parallel vs Distributed Computing
content.definition:
Sequential: one operation at a time, time = sum of all steps.
Parallel: some operations run simultaneously on one system, time = sequential time + longest parallel task.
Distributed: multiple devices run the program, solves problems too large or slow for one computer.

content.term: Benefits of Parallel and Distributed Computing
content.definition: Parallel computing solutions can scale more effectively than sequential solutions. Distributed computing allows problems to be solved that could not be solved on a single computer due to processing time or storage needs, and allows much larger problems to be solved more quickly.

rows: Some operations run simultaneously on one system
Multiple separate devices each run part of the program
Varies — depends on how work is divided
Can it run on one computer?
Medium problems that can be broken into independent parts
Very large problems that exceed one computer's processing or storage capacity
Poor — adding hardware does not help
Good — more processors reduce parallel portion time
Excellent — add more machines as problems grow

content.text: A programmer needs to process a data set. The program has the following structure: load data (8 seconds, must run first), process chunk A (30 seconds), process chunk B (45 seconds), process chunk C (20 seconds), combine results (5 seconds, must run last). Chunks A, B, and C can run simultaneously.

content.code:
-- Sequential time:
8 + 30 + 45 + 20 + 5 = 108 seconds

-- Parallel time:
-- Sequential portion: load (8s) + combine (5s) = 13s
-- Parallel portion: max(30s, 45s, 20s) = 45s (chunk B is longest)
-- Total parallel time = 13 + 45 = 58 seconds

-- Speedup:
Speedup = sequential time / parallel time
Speedup = 108 / 58 ≈ 1.86
The parallel solution is about 1.86 times faster.

-- What if we add more processors? Chunks A, B, C can be split further?
-- Even with INFINITE processors for A, B, C:
-- Minimum time = sequential portion = 13 seconds (cannot be improved)
-- Maximum possible speedup = 108 / 13 ≈ 8.3×

content.label: Common Mistake
content.text: Students often add ALL parallel task times together instead of taking only the LONGEST. In the example above, chunks A (30s), B (45s), and C (20s) run SIMULTANEOUSLY — so only 45 seconds pass (the longest), not 30+45+20=95 seconds. The shorter tasks finish while the longest is still running.
Summary: What to Know for the Exam

items: Sequential computing: operations performed in order one at a time; total time = sum of ALL steps
Parallel computing: some operations performed simultaneously; total time = sequential tasks + LONGEST parallel task
Distributed computing: multiple devices run a program; solves problems too large or slow for one computer
Comparing efficiency: compare the time each approach takes to perform the same task
A speedup of 4 means the parallel solution is 4 times faster than the sequential solution
Every parallel solution has BOTH a parallel portion AND a sequential portion
Parallel computing solutions can scale more effectively than sequential solutions
At some point, adding more parallel processes will no longer meaningfully increase efficiency because the sequential portion becomes the bottleneck
The sequential portion sets a ceiling on the maximum possible speedup regardless of how many processors are added
Distributed computing allows problems to be solved that could NOT be solved on a single computer due to processing time or storage needs
Distributed computing allows much larger problems to be solved more quickly than with a single computer
